articles.headline: Kubernetes v1.37 pushes HPA scale‑to‑zero into the core as a beta‑by‑default feature
articles.dek: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler now ships in the main API, can drop workloads to zero pods, and stays active while the service buffers traffic.

body.text: Key Takeaway

Kubernetes 1.37 moves the HorizontalPodAutoscaler’s scale‑to‑zero mode out of alpha and into the core API as a beta feature that’s enabled by default.  The HPA controller now lives inside the main repo and you no longer need an external component to use it. [FACT:212be6ff2deb5b228e593ec9e907ba16] [FACT:251265d562f1a46c1ec812d4ed228a29] [FACT:1fcd7f56e8347786cf28a72f43f7e9c1] [FACT:321254c16862e7aac3ac96430bd49429]
Why This Matters

Builders can finally let idle services spin completely down, saving cloud‑provider dollars, while the built‑in Service continues to accept requests and hold them until a new pod spins up.  The last idle pod is removed as soon as the replica count hits zero. [FACT:ad9f1fa73c6946f84840f29be6d48a5b] [FACT:24a3e192fd788e6929fa1f679e9665c5]
What Happened

The v1.37 release adds native support for the HPA’s zero‑scale mode, integrates the controller into the core codebase, and flips the feature flag to beta‑by‑default.  In earlier releases you had to install an external metrics adapter to get any autoscaling at all. [FACT:212be6ff2deb5b228e593ec9e907ba16] [FACT:321254c16862e7aac3ac96430bd49429] [FACT:1fcd7f56e8347786cf28a72f43f7e9c1]
Builder View

Add `minReplicas: 0` to an HPA spec, watch the replica count drop to zero when CPU or custom metrics dip, and trust the Service layer to buffer inbound traffic.  Metrics are still sourced from the running pods while they exist, so scaling decisions remain accurate.  Once a request arrives, the Service spawns a new pod and hands the request over. [FACT:ad9f1fa73c6946f84840f29be6d48a5b] [FACT:3d188ed25640102e5421035b21860322] [FACT:24a3e192fd788e6929fa1f679e9665c5]
Open Questions

Open items include measuring cold‑start latency for the first pod after a zero‑scale event, determining how large the Service’s request buffer can grow under burst traffic, and the timeline for graduating the feature to GA.  The current docs note that once the replica count hits zero the Service continues to queue requests, but real‑world limits are still being profiled. [FACT:24a3e192fd788e6929fa1f679e9665c5] [FACT:80f0e92ee5580ea08acf81caad56494b]
Ardur Take

Turn the beta flag on (it’s on by default), set `minReplicas: 0` on HPAs you want to discount, and run a quick load test.  The cost reduction is immediate, and the risk is low enough to trial in production if you already have readiness probes in place.  Keep an eye on pod churn metrics and the Service buffer size during the test. [FACT:212be6ff2deb5b228e593ec9e907ba16] [FACT:251265d562f1a46c1ec812d4ed228a29]

keyPoints: HPA scale‑to‑zero is now a core, beta‑by‑default feature in v1.37.
No external metrics adapter is required; the controller lives in the main repo.
Services continue to accept traffic while pods are at zero, then spin a pod up on demand.
articles.whyItMatters: Saving compute when workloads are idle directly reduces cloud spend, and the built‑in request buffering means you don’t have to redesign services to survive zero‑replica periods.
articles.readerAction: Enable the beta flag (if it isn’t already), update your HPA manifests with `minReplicas: 0`, deploy to a staging cluster, and monitor the scaling behavior and request queue length.
